sections.abstract: The paper introduces a coreset spectral clustering (CSC) algorithm designed to scale spectral clustering to large datasets. By exploiting the equivalence between kernel $k$-means and the normalized cut problem, the authors combine the benefits of coresets with spectral clustering. The main contribution is an algorithm that clusters a coreset graph to infer labels for the original graph, proving that an $\alpha$-approximation on the coreset yields an $O(\alpha)$-approximation on the original. Additionally, they improve coreset construction time for sparse kernels from $\tilde{O}(nk)$ to $\tilde{O}(n \cdot \min\{k, d_{avg}\})$. Experiments on graphs up to 65 million nodes demonstrate superior speed and accuracy compared to existing coreset kernel $k$-means methods.
sections.introduction: Kernel $k$-means and spectral clustering are popular for non-linear decision boundaries but are often studied separately despite their objective functions being equivalent up to a constant factor. Spectral clustering speedups typically involve graph sparsification, while kernel $k$-means utilizes coresets to make costs independent of $n$. This paper proposes a unified approach: a faster coreset construction for sparse kernels and a CSC algorithm that solves the coreset problem using spectral clustering. This methodology avoids the local minima issues common in kernel $k$-means while maintaining the efficiency of coreset-based methods.
sections.method: The paper defines the kernel matrix $K = \Phi^T \Phi$ and squared distance $\Delta(\phi(x), \phi(y)) \triangleq \|\phi(x) - \phi(y)\|^2$. Key definitions include centroids $c_w^\phi(\pi_j) = (\sum_{x \in \pi_j} w(x)\phi(x)) / (\sum_{x \in \pi_j} w(x))$, the kernel $k$-means objective $\text{COST}_w^\phi(X, C) = \sum_{x \in X} w(x)\Delta(\phi(x), C)$, and the normalized cut objective $\text{NC}(G, \Pi) = \frac{1}{k} \sum_{j=1}^k \Phi_G(\pi_j)$. The authors improve coreset construction to $\tilde{O}(m)$ time for sparse kernels by exploiting the property: $\Delta(x, C) = \begin{cases} \Delta(x, x^*) & x \not\sim c \text{ for all } c \in C \\ \min_{c \in C} \Delta(x, c) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \quad (3)$. The CSC algorithm converts the normalized cut problem to weighted kernel $k$-means ($K = D^{-1}AD^{-1}, W = D$), constructs an $\epsilon$-coreset, and solves the cut on the coreset graph $A_H = W_H K(V') W_H$. Theorem 1 guarantees: $\text{NC}_{A_G, D_G}(\Pi') \le \alpha \cdot \frac{1 + \epsilon}{1 - \epsilon} \cdot \text{OPTNC}_{A_G, D_G}(k)$.
sections.experiments: Experiments compared the new coreset construction against previous methods on large-scale graphs including Friendster (65M nodes), LiveJournal (4M nodes), and wiki-topcats (2M nodes). Clustering performance was evaluated on MNIST, PenDigits, HAR, and Letter datasets using CSC variants against full spectral clustering and coreset kernel $k$-means. Synthetic tests utilized a stochastic block model where the number of clusters $k$ was proportional to $n$ to test scalability up to 250 clusters.
sections.results: The new coreset construction is significantly faster on sparse graphs, matching theoretical expectations. CSC variants performed as well as full spectral clustering using coresets less than 5% of the original size. CSC significantly outperformed coreset kernel $k$-means, which struggled with local optima as $k$ increased. In synthetic tests, CSC scaled to 250 clusters with an ARI of 0.5 in under 3 seconds, whereas coreset kernel $k$-means became ineffective after 50 clusters.
sections.supplementary: The supplementary material provides detailed plots for ARI and Normalized Cut across various datasets. It includes formal proofs for the equivalence of kernel $k$-means and trace-based objectives, and the approximation bounds for Theorem 1. Full pseudocode is provided for the coreset framework and subroutines: Algorithm 6 (CONSTRUCTT) for building the sampling tree, Algorithm 7 (REPAIR) for efficient tree updates exploiting sparsity, and Algorithm 8 (SAMPLEPOINT) for $O(\log n)$ sampling.
